title: What information is worth
objectives: Price information as the expected gain from deciding after seeing it.

screens.title: One look
screens.prose: Three face-down cards: one is worth £90, the others nothing. You will take one card. First you may turn one over. You turned card A: it shows £0.
screens.question: Tap the card you take now.

hints.text: Card A is known to be worthless.
The £90 is behind B or C, equally likely.
Take either B or C.

feedback.correct: Either B or C: each now hides the £90 with chance one half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a card that might still be the prize.

byKey.seen: Card A is face up at £0. Take one of the two that may hold the £90.

explain.text: Turning A showed £0, so the prize is B or C, each with chance one half. Had A shown £90, you would take it. Either way the look changed what you do.

screens.title: What the look is worth
screens.prose: Compare the game with and without the look. Without it you pick a card blind.
screens.question: Fill in the three values, in £.

rows: The game with one look first

hints.text: Blind: £90 with chance $\tfrac13$.
With a look: you win if the look finds the prize ($\tfrac13$), or else half the time ($\tfrac23 \times \tfrac12$).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out your chance of the prize in each case.

byKey.r1c1: The look finds the prize a third of the time; otherwise you pick one of two. $\tfrac13 + \tfrac23 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac23$, so £60.
byKey.r2c1: The look is worth the difference: £60 with it, £30 without.

explain.text: Blind, you win £90 a third of the time: £30. With a look you win $\tfrac13 + \tfrac23 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac23$ of the time: £60. The **value of information** is the gain from deciding after seeing it: £30.

screens.title: Knowing the outcome
screens.prose: A trade makes £30 or loses £20, each with chance one half. You can take it now or skip it. Suppose someone could tell you the outcome first.
screens.question: What is perfect information about the outcome worth, in £?

hints.text: Now: take it for $\tfrac12(30) + \tfrac12(-20)$.
Told the outcome, you take only the winners: $\tfrac12 \times 30$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the value with the information, then take away the value now.

byKey.fifteen: £15 is the value with the information. Take away the £5 you get anyway.
byKey.thirty: £30 is the best outcome. You learn it only half the time.

explain.text: Now the trade is worth $15 - 10 = £5$, so you take it. Told the outcome, you take the winners only: $\tfrac12 \times 30 = £15$. Perfect information is worth £10, the most any message about this trade can be worth.

screens.title: An analyst who is right 80% of the time
screens.prose: An analyst calls the same trade good or bad and is right 80% of the time. A good call comes half the time. Work out your best move after each call.
screens.question: Fill in the table.

hints.text: After a good call the trade wins with chance 0.8; after a bad call, 0.2.
Good: $0.8 \times 30 - 0.2 \times 20 = 20$. Bad: $0.2 \times 30 - 0.8 \times 20 = -10$, so skip.
With the analyst $0.5 \times 20 = 10$, against 5 now: worth 5.

feedback.correct: Take after a good call (+£20), skip after a bad one; the analyst is worth £5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the trade's value after each message, then take the better move.

byKey.r1c3: After a bad call the trade is worth −£10, so you skip it: £0.
byKey.r2c3: With the analyst you expect $0.5 \times 20 + 0.5 \times 0 = 10$. Without, £5. The difference is £5.

explain.text: A good call makes the trade worth £20, a bad call −£10, so you skip after a bad call. That gives £10 on average, against £5 now: the analyst is worth £5. A simulation of 400,000 trades lands within a penny of £10.

screens.title: Right most of the time
screens.prose: A new trade makes £50 or loses £10, each with chance one half. The same 80% analyst offers to call it.
screens.question: What is the analyst worth to you?

options.text: £0: you take the trade whatever he says
Something: he is right 80% of the time
options.why: Accuracy is not enough. After a bad call the trade is still worth +£2, so you take it anyway.
£20 is what the trade earns without him. He adds nothing to it.

hints.text: Work out the trade's value after a bad call.
Still positive: you take it after either call.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether a bad call would make you skip.

byKey.b: Accuracy is not enough. After a bad call the trade is still worth +£2, so you take it anyway.

explain.text: After a bad call the trade is worth $0.2 \times 50 - 0.8 \times 10 = +£2$, so you still take it. You would take it after a good call too. Information that cannot change your decision is worth nothing.

screens.title: A weaker analyst
screens.prose: Back to the trade that makes £30 or loses £20. Two weaker analysts: one right 60% of the time, one right 70%.
screens.question: What is each analyst worth, in £?

hints.text: After a bad call from the 60% analyst: $0.4 \times 30 - 0.6 \times 20$.
That is exactly 0: skipping is no better than taking.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the trade's value after a bad call from each analyst.

byKey.r0c1: After his bad call the trade is worth $12 - 12 = 0$, so skipping gains nothing. He is worth £0.
byKey.r1c1: After a bad call: $9 - 14 = -5$, skip. After a good one: $21 - 6 = 15$. So $0.5 \times 15 = 7.5$, against 5 now.

explain.text: The 60% analyst's bad call leaves the trade at exactly £0, so it never improves your move. The 70% analyst's bad call makes it −£5, so you skip: $7.50 - 5 = £2.50$. Accuracy pays only past the point where a message flips the decision.

screens.title: Decide after you see it
screens.prose:
The value of information is the expected payoff when you decide after seeing it, less the best payoff deciding now:

$$\text{VOI} = E\left[\max_a E[\text{payoff} \mid \text{message}]\right] - \max_a E[\text{payoff}]$$

It is never negative and never above the value of perfect information.
screens.question: When is a piece of information worth exactly nothing?

options.text: When no message could change your decision
When it is wrong some of the time
options.why: The 80% analyst was worth £5 though often wrong. What matters is whether he changes your move.

options.text: When the trade is already worth taking
options.why: The +£30 or −£20 trade was worth taking, yet the 80% analyst added £5.

hints.text: Information is worth the decisions it changes.
If every message leads to the same move, the max does not move.
When no message changes the decision.

feedback.correct: When no message could change your decision.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the information is used for.

explain.text: Information pays only through better decisions. If every message leads to the move you would make anyway, it is worth £0. Otherwise it is worth something, up to the value of knowing everything.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three questions, about two minutes each, as a senior trader would ask them. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers, in £.

rows: A die pays its face in £, or take £3 instead. What is seeing the roll first worth?
Lesson 12's river spot (you win 6 of 25 combos, £50 into £100): calling only when ahead earns
The 80% analyst on the +£30 or −£20 trade: the most you would pay

hints.text: Die: compare $E[\max(X, 3)]$ with $\max(E[X], 3)$.
River: win £150 on the 6 combos you beat, else fold.
0.50, 36 and 5; so at £6, do not buy.

feedback.correct: £0.50, £36 and £5: do not pay £6 for the analyst.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Seeing it, you take $\max(X, 3)$: $\tfrac{3 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6}{6} = 4$. Blind, the die is worth 3.50, more than £3.
byKey.r1c1: You call only the 6 combos you beat: $\tfrac{6}{25} \times 150 = 36$. Folding the rest costs nothing.

explain.text: The die: $E[\max(X, 3)] = £4$ against £3.50 blind, so £0.50. Seeing his cards: $\tfrac{6}{25} \times 150 = £36$, against £0 for folding. The analyst is worth £5, so at £6 you do not buy.

screens.title: Follow-up: a tell
screens.prose: The interviewer returns to lesson 12's river: 6 of 25 combos win, £50 into £100, so folding is right. Now you spot a tell that is right 80% of the time: it reads weak or strong.
screens.question: What is the tell worth, in £?

hints.text: Call after weak, fold after strong.
Weak and you win: $0.24 \times 0.8 = 0.192$; weak and you lose: $0.76 \times 0.2 = 0.152$.

feedback.correct: £21.20: call on weak, fold on strong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Call only when the tell reads weak, then weight the outcomes.

byKey.cards: £36 is for seeing his cards, perfect information. An 80% tell is worth less.
byKey.both: You weighted only the wins after a weak read. Take off the £50 lost in 0.152 of hands.

explain.text: After a weak read (chance $\tfrac{43}{125}$) you win $\tfrac{24}{43} = 55.8\%$, so call; after strong, only $\tfrac{3}{41}$, so fold. The tell is worth $0.192 \times 150 - 0.152 \times 50 = £21.20$, against £36 for the cards. Waiting for the next card is the same gain, as in `graphs-dp` l17.

ideas: The value of information is the payoff deciding after seeing it, less the best payoff deciding now.
It is never negative and never more than the value of perfect information.
It is zero when no message could change your decision, however accurate the source.
summary.trap: Paying for accuracy. A source that is right 80% of the time is worth nothing if it never changes your move.

quiz.prose: A trade makes £40 with chance 0.6 or loses £40 with chance 0.4. You may take it or skip it.
quiz.question: What is perfect information about the outcome worth, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value with the information, less the value now.

byKey.with: £24 is the value with perfect information. Take away the £8 you get anyway.
byKey.now: £8 is the trade's value now, not the information's.

explain.text: Now the trade is worth $24 - 16 = £8$. Told the outcome, you take only winners: $0.6 \times 40 = £24$. Perfect information is worth £16.

quiz.prose: Whatever a report says, you will make the same trade.
quiz.question: What is the report worth?

options.text: Its accuracy times the trade's value
options.why: Accuracy matters only if a message could change what you do.

options.text: Something, since more information never hurts
options.why: It never hurts, but here it never helps either: your move is fixed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the report could change.

explain.text: Information is worth the decisions it improves. If every message leads to the same trade, it improves none. So it is worth £0.

quiz.prose: You may bet £10 at evens on a fair coin, or decline.
quiz.question: What is it worth to see the coin first, in £?

widget.accept: 5: you bet only when you would win.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value with the look, less the value without.

byKey.ten: £10 is the win when you bet. You see a winner only half the time.

explain.text: Blind, the bet is worth £0. Seeing the coin, you bet only on a winner: $\tfrac12 \times 10 = £5$. So the look is worth £5.
